topics.title: 4.1 Unsigned Integers
topics.summary: An unsigned w -bit value interprets every bit as a nonnegative positional weight. The value is the sum of b_i * 2^i over positions 0 through w-1 . There is no sign bit in this interpretation. Every pattern represents a value. For eight bits, 11111111 is 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255 . This direct relationship makes unsigned types useful for masks, counters with explicitly modular behavior, and binary fields. It does not make unsigned the best choice for every ordinary quantity, especially where negative error indicators or differences are meaningful. The minimum unsigned value is zero. The maximum is 2^w - 1 , because the sum of all positional weights below 2^w is one less than 2^w . An eight-bit unsigned type spans 0 through 255; a 16-bit type spans 0 through 65,535. The number of values is one greater than the maximum because zero is included. This matters in capacity calculations and exhaustive tests. A field described as “eight bits” provides 256 distinct patterns, but a protocol may reserve some of them, reducing the set of valid application values. Unsigned arithmetic is performed modulo 2^w for the relevant unsigned type. Mathematically, values differing by a multiple of 2^w map to the same representation. In eight-bit arithmetic, 250 + 10 maps to 4 because 260 - 256 = 4 . Integer promotions can cause a small unsigned type’s expression to be evaluated in a wider signed type first. Assigning the result back to the narrow unsigned type still performs the specified conversion. State whether a trace is describing an eight-bit mathematical model or the exact promoted type of a C expression. The final stored pattern may agree even when the intermediate language operations differ.

topics.title: 4.2 Signed Integers
topics.summary: Two’s complement assigns the high bit a negative weight. A w -bit pattern has value -b_(w-1)*2^(w-1) + sum(b_i*2^i) for the remaining positions. The range is -2^(w-1) through 2^(w-1)-1 . There is one more negative value than positive nonzero values. This is the representation used by the reference platform and required by C++20’s signed integer representation rules. C17 permits additional signed representations, so statements about their byte patterns must be treated as platform assumptions in a C17 program. Representation does not change the rule that overflowing ordinary signed arithmetic is undefined. In two’s complement, the most significant bit distinguishes nonnegative and negative values, but it is not an independent minus-sign flag. Flipping that bit alone does not generally negate the number. It changes the contribution of a power-of-two weight. For an eight-bit value, 00000101 is 5, while 10000101 is -128 + 5 = -123 , not -5. The representation of -5 is 11111011 . This is why sign-magnitude intuition gives incorrect results when interpreting ordinary machine integers. Nonnegative two’s-complement values have a zero high bit and the same low-bit encoding as their unsigned values. Eight-bit 37 is 00100101 . This shared encoding makes many machine operations work naturally for both signed and unsigned data, with the interpretation of flags or comparisons providing the difference. The largest positive eight-bit value is 01111111 , or 127. Incrementing it in a raw eight-bit hardware operation produces the pattern 10000000 . That observation does not license a C or C++ signed expression to overflow. The source-language contract and machine result must remain separate. A negative two’s-complement pattern can be interpreted by subtracting 2^w from its unsigned interpretation. For eight bits, 11110011 is 243 unsigned and 243 - 256 = -13 signed. This is often the quickest way to decode a negative pattern by hand. The minimum value has only the high bit set: 10000000 is -128. There is no positive 128 in the same signed type. This asymmetry is responsible for special cases in negation, absolute value, and division. Boundary tests should include the minimum, not merely small negative values. At the bit-pattern level, two’s-complement negation in a fixed width is obtained by inverting the bits and adding one, with the result reduced to that width. For eight-bit 13, 00001101 becomes 11110010 , then 11110011 , representing -13. The minimum value maps to its own pattern under this modular operation. In signed source arithmetic, negating the minimum is not representable and therefore is not a valid ordinary signed result. An absolute-value routine must check or use a representation that can hold the positive magnitude. Do not assume abs(x) is safe for every value of a signed type.

topics.title: 4.4 Integer Arithmetic
topics.summary: Unsigned addition wraps according to its type. Signed addition requires the mathematical result to be representable. To check nonnegative unsigned addition before performing it, test b <= maximum - a . For signed addition, use separate positive and negative cases or a documented checked-arithmetic facility. Checking after a signed overflow is too late. An expression such as if (a + b < a) cannot reliably detect signed overflow because the addition itself may already violate the language’s requirements. Validate the operation’s precondition, not merely the resulting pattern. Unsigned subtraction also wraps. If an unsigned count is zero, subtracting one produces the maximum value, not -1. This is the classic failure in a reverse loop whose condition is i >= 0 : the condition is always true for an unsigned i . For lengths, subtraction is often safer than addition only after the order is established. To validate a region, first require offset <= total , then require length <= total - offset . This avoids overflow in offset + length while preventing unsigned underflow in the subtraction. Allocation and indexing frequently multiply a count by an element size. The product must fit before it is passed to an allocator. For nonzero s , require count <= SIZE_MAX / s . Then count * s is representable as size_t . A successful allocation of a wrapped, too-small product is more dangerous than a clean allocation failure. The code may later write the original number of elements into the undersized block. Treat multiplication validation as part of memory safety, not merely numerical correctness. Integer division discards a fractional part. For signed division in the language versions used here, truncation is toward zero: -7 / 3 is -2. The remainder satisfies a == (a/b)*b + a%b when the operations are defined, and its sign follows the dividend when nonzero. Division by zero is invalid. Dividing the minimum signed value by -1 is also invalid when the positive quotient cannot be represented. A checked division must handle both cases. Unsigned division does not have the signed-minimum case, but still requires a nonzero divisor. Overflow means the mathematical result exceeds the representable range. The consequence depends on the operation and type. Unsigned modular arithmetic is defined. Ordinary signed overflow is undefined. A machine instruction may set a carry or overflow flag, but an ordinary source expression does not automatically expose or check that flag. Use a tested checked-arithmetic routine when values approach limits. Compiler built-ins can help on supported compilers, but they are not part of the portable C17 or C++20 core interface. A library boundary should report range failure explicitly rather than returning a plausible wrapped size. For integers, “underflow” is often used informally for a result below the minimum representable value. Unsigned 0 - 1 wraps; signed subtraction below the minimum is undefined. Floating-point underflow has a different technical meaning involving tiny results, discussed in Chapter 5. Use precise language in diagnostics. “Negative length rejected” is more useful than “underflow happened” when the actual failure is invalid input. The distinction helps identify whether the fix belongs in input validation, type selection, or arithmetic checking. Wraparound is the cycling of a finite modular value through its range. It can be useful for checksums, sequence counters, and ring indices, but only when the algorithm is designed for it. Comparing modular sequence numbers requires a defined window of ambiguity; ordinary numeric order is not automatically the desired temporal order. For a ring of arbitrary capacity, index = (index + 1) % capacity is conceptually clear but still requires nonzero capacity and a representable increment. If the capacity is a power of two and the index domain is controlled, masking can implement the wrap. The optimization follows from the invariant; it does not replace it.

topics.title: Worked example — Checking a byte-count calculation
topics.summary: Suppose an input requests 1,500 records, each occupying 24 bytes, plus a 64-byte header. The required calculation is header + count*stride . The order of checks must prevent both multiplication and addition overflow. Companion listing: ch04/checked_size.cpp The multiplication produces 36,000. Adding 64 produces 36,064. The first guard ensures that the multiplication is valid in the size domain, while the second guard ensures that the header fits in the remaining range. A zero stride is allowed by this mathematical helper; an application can impose a stricter semantic rule before calling it. Now consider a count larger than maximum / 24 . The function rejects it before multiplying. This is the recovery boundary: no allocation has occurred and no partial object exists. A tempting alternative, multiplying first and checking whether the result looks small, is harder to reason about and easy to get wrong when signed types or additional arithmetic enter the expression.

reading.title: Where the simple approach fails
paragraphs: Checking count * width only after multiplication may observe a wrapped unsigned result. Signed overflow is undefined behavior.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Multiply first and compare the result with limit. An unsigned wrapped result can be small enough to pass.
